title: Intelligent Tutors Beyond K-12: An Observational Study of Adult Learner Engagement and Academic Impact
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether intelligent tutoring systems, which have mostly been studied in K-12 settings, can also benefit adult learners in postsecondary education when use is voluntary rather than required. The authors focus on two questions: how optional tutor use relates to adult learners’ academic outcomes, and what demographic or behavioral characteristics distinguish adults who choose to use intelligent tutors.

The intervention studied is the Apprentice Tutors platform, a set of adaptive College Algebra tutors integrated into Blackboard and Canvas via LTI at a state technical college. The tutors provided real-time correctness feedback, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing-based adaptive problem selection, multi-layered hints, progress tracking, tutorial videos, links to textbook and YouTube resources, and a bug/Q&A feature. The study analyzed two years of platform deployment data, combining tutor interaction logs with institutional grades and demographic records. Analyses included descriptive statistics, usage analyses, learning-curve modeling, and regression analysis.

The population was adult learners enrolled in College Algebra at a 2-year state technical college in the United States, many of whom balanced work with night, hybrid, in-person, or online study. The dataset included 3,510 students overall, with 520 students using the tutors at least once and 214 using them in Unit 1, which had the greatest tutor coverage. Tutor users were more likely to be female and slightly older than non-users, and usage was concentrated in evenings, late nights, and on Thursdays, suggesting that flexibility mattered for this learner population.

The main conclusion is that voluntary use of intelligent tutors appears promising for adult postsecondary learners. Students showed reduced error rates with more practice inside the tutors, and tutor use was positively associated with higher Unit 1 assessment scores outside the tutor. However, because the study was observational and lacked random assignment, the authors emphasize that these findings are preliminary and do not establish causality. They argue that intelligent tutors are a viable supplementary resource for adult learners and recommend future randomized studies and broader tutor coverage to test long-term and more generalizable effects.
